Time Magazine. Founded in 1923 by Henry Luce and Briton Hadden, it revolutionized American journalism by condensing the week's news into a digestible, lively format. The first issue was published on March 3, 1923. The magazine pioneered the news-summary magazine concept and became the most influential publication of the twentieth century, shaping how millions understood current events. Time created the distinctive Time style, employing short, snappy paragraphs, vivid reporting, and irreverent commentary that made news engaging rather than dry. The magazine introduced the Man of the Year tradition in 1927, later called Person of the Year, naming outstanding figures of the previous year. Circulation climbed to over three million by the 1950s, making Time essential reading for educated Americans. The magazine became famous for innovative layouts, color photography, and the Time style red border on the cover that became instantly recognizable. Henry Luce built Time Incorporated, a media empire that later included Life, Fortune, and Sports Illustrated. The magazine maintained a conservative editorial stance during the Cold War while claiming objectivity as a news digest. Time pioneered the news-magazine format and shaped public understanding of world events throughout the twentieth century.
